goal: Move from the felt uncertainty of a coin flip to the information measures that explain compression, prediction, dependence, model mismatch, and reliable communication.

lessons.objective: By the end you can describe a coin flip as a random experiment with possible outcomes and explain why a short run need not alternate.

beats.text: A coin is suspended between heads and tails. Before it lands, there are two live possibilities, and a single answer will remove that uncertainty.
If ten flips happen to contain seven heads, does the next flip owe us tails, or can it still be independent?
Label each outcome and collect many independent flips. The labels stay unpredictable one at a time while the running fraction begins to reveal a stable distribution.
Random does not mean patternless: probability describes the long-run weighting of outcomes without dictating the next result.
A coin is a tiny information source. Every message it emits will later be measured by how much uncertainty it removes.
Keep two ideas: a random variable has possible outcomes with probabilities, and independent trials do not compensate for earlier luck.

visuals.title: The two-door coin
visuals.goal: Make two live possibilities and independent short runs intuitive.

visuals.title: Flip tree
visuals.goal: Draw a binary branch for each successive flip.

visuals.title: Coin-flip information lab
visuals.goal: Compare empirical frequencies for fair and biased coins.

lessons.objective: By the end you can assign and interpret probabilities that sum to one and distinguish a long-run frequency from a guarantee about a short run.

beats.text: Two coins look alike, but one is balanced and one is weighted. Their labels are the same; their probability distributions are different.
What does p(heads)=0.7 actually promise, and what does it leave open about the next ten flips?
Place probability mass into mutually exclusive buckets and require the buckets to add to one. Simulate trials and watch the observed fraction wobble around its target.
Probability weights possibilities before an observation; frequency is evidence collected after many observations. A probability is not a countdown to an exact quota.
Once possibilities have weights, we can ask a sharper question: how much information arrives when one weighted possibility is selected?
A probability lies between zero and one, exclusive outcomes sum to one, and repeated frequencies tend to reflect the assigned probabilities.

visuals.title: Probability pie
visuals.goal: Show probability as weighted possibility mass.

visuals.title: Mass conservation
visuals.goal: Keep the total probability at one while moving weight between outcomes.

lessons.objective: By the end you can compute an outcome's surprise as -log₂ p and explain why rarer outcomes carry more bits.

beats.text: A friend says the sun rose today. Another says a six-digit secret code matched by chance. Both are true, but they do not feel equally informative.
What numerical rule turns a probability into a quantity of information while making independent surprises add?
Imagine locating an outcome by asking fair yes-or-no questions. An event with probability one needs no questions; an event with probability one-half needs one on average.
The rule is I(x) = -log₂ p(x). Halving probability adds one bit, so probability one-eighth means three bits of surprise.
The logarithm changes multiplication of independent probabilities into addition of information, matching how question counts concatenate.
Surprise belongs to an outcome, equals -log₂ of its probability, is zero for certainty, and grows as the outcome becomes rare.

visuals.title: The rare-message ladder
visuals.goal: Make -log₂ p feel like the number of binary questions required.

visuals.title: Question tree
visuals.goal: Show one extra binary fork for each halving of probability.

lessons.objective: By the end you can calculate expected surprise by weighting each outcome's surprise by how often it occurs.

beats.text: A source sometimes whispers a common word and rarely shouts an extraordinary one. The shout is more surprising, but the whisper happens more often.
What should we call the average number of information bits delivered per message over a long stream?
Write each outcome's surprise beside its probability, multiply the two, and add all products. Frequent outcomes contribute repeatedly; rare outcomes contribute a large amount when they appear.
Expected surprise is E[I(X)] = Σ p(x)(-log₂ p(x)). It is a probability-weighted average, not simply the largest surprise.
The same expectation will become entropy when the outcome variable is named X: uncertainty can be averaged before or after we call it information.
To average surprise, multiply each surprise by its probability and sum. The result predicts long-run information per emitted symbol.

visuals.title: The weighted surprise scale
visuals.goal: Show why common and rare outcomes both matter to an average.

visuals.title: Probability-weighted bars
visuals.goal: Compare p(x) with I(x) before multiplying them.

lessons.objective: By the end you can compute Shannon entropy and explain why a uniform distribution has the greatest uncertainty for a fixed number of outcomes.

beats.text: Two boxes each contain one of four symbols. In one box every symbol is equally likely; in the other, one symbol dominates. Which box is harder to predict?
Can one number capture the average uncertainty of an entire probability distribution rather than one observed event?
Reuse the expected-surprise calculation for a random variable X: H(X) = -Σ p(x)log₂ p(x). Move probability mass while keeping the number of labels fixed.
Entropy peaks when mass is spread uniformly and falls when mass concentrates. The formula is expected surprise measured in binary questions.
Entropy is a property of a distribution, not of a single outcome. It predicts the average coding effort before the next symbol is seen.
Entropy is expected surprise, uses -Σp log₂p, and reaches its maximum when all allowed outcomes are equally likely.

visuals.title: Uncertainty landscapes
visuals.goal: Contrast concentrated and uniform probability mass.

visuals.title: Entropy surface
visuals.goal: Plot entropy of a binary source as p moves from 0 to 1.

visuals.title: Coin-flip information lab
visuals.goal: Bias the coin and connect each outcome's frequency and surprise to the entropy of the source.

lessons.objective: By the end you can interpret a bit as one fair binary choice and convert between bits of entropy and average binary decisions.

beats.text: A single yes-or-no answer chooses one branch of a fork. That fork is the smallest useful measuring stick for information.
Why does base 2 make the unit of entropy a bit, and why is a fair coin exactly one bit?
Build a binary decision tree. One level separates two equally likely outcomes; two levels separate four; each level adds one binary decision.
A bit is one binary digit and one fair binary choice. A fair coin has H = -2(1/2)log₂(1/2) = 1 bit per flip.
Choosing another logarithm base changes the unit, while the underlying uncertainty stays the same; base 2 is natural for digital codes.
Bits count binary alternatives. One fair binary choice carries one bit, and entropy in base 2 predicts average bits per symbol.

visuals.title: One fork, one bit
visuals.goal: Connect binary branches to the unit of information.

visuals.title: Binary question tree
visuals.goal: Count tree depth as bits of information.

lessons.objective: By the end you can explain cross-entropy as the average number of bits assigned by a model Q to data generated by P.

beats.text: A weather forecaster predicts tomorrow using the wrong climate model. Even when the forecast is plausible, its code words may be longer than necessary.
How can we score predictions when reality follows P but the predictor assigns probabilities Q?
For each outcome, charge -log₂ Q(x), then average those charges using the real source probabilities p(x). The scorer asks how surprised Q is by P's messages.
Cross-entropy H(P,Q) = Eₚ[-log₂Q(x)]. It is the expected code length when a Q-shaped code is used on P-shaped data.
Using Q=P gives ordinary entropy. Any mismatch makes the average bill no smaller, with severe punishment for predictions that assign nearly zero probability to events that occur.
Cross-entropy uses P to average and Q inside the surprise. It measures predictive or coding cost under a possibly wrong model.

visuals.title: The forecast bill
visuals.goal: Make cross-entropy an average prediction cost.

visuals.title: Two coding trees
visuals.goal: Compare ideal P code lengths with Q-assigned lengths.

lessons.objective: By the end you can read joint entropy as the average information needed to identify a pair of outcomes together.

beats.text: A weather report has two fields: sky and wind. Reading both together creates a larger answer than reading either field alone.
How many bits are needed on average to identify the row and column of a paired outcome?
Lay joint probabilities into a grid. Each cell is one pair (x,y), and the entropy formula treats those cells as the outcomes of one larger random variable.
H(X,Y) = -Σ p(x,y)log₂p(x,y). It is symmetric in X and Y and can be smaller than H(X)+H(Y) when the variables share structure.
A pair can be identified in stages: ask about X, then ask what remains about Y. That staged view leads directly to conditional entropy and the chain rule.
Joint entropy treats pairs as combined outcomes, counts bits to identify both, and reflects dependence through the joint probabilities.

visuals.title: The probability grid
visuals.goal: Turn paired outcomes into cells whose entropy can be counted.

visuals.title: Joint distribution grid
visuals.goal: Compare independent and diagonal joint distributions.

lessons.objective: By the end you can interpret H(Y|X) as uncertainty remaining after X is observed and use the chain rule for a pair.

beats.text: A clue reveals the weather at noon. The wind is still uncertain, but less of the original possibility cloud remains.
How many more bits are needed to identify Y after the receiver already knows X?
For each value of X, inspect the conditional distribution of Y. Compute its entropy, then average those entropies according to how often each X occurs.
H(Y|X) is the uncertainty left in Y after X. The chain rule H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X) adds the first-stage and remaining questions.
Conditioning cannot increase average uncertainty: a clue can leave the same fog or remove some, but it cannot make the original prediction harder in expectation.
Conditional entropy is leftover uncertainty, is generally directional, and completes joint entropy through the chain rule.

visuals.title: The clue that clears fog
visuals.goal: Show uncertainty shrinking after a condition is known.

visuals.title: Conditional question tree
visuals.goal: Separate H(X) from the remaining H(Y|X).

lessons.objective: By the end you can calculate mutual information as the uncertainty about one variable removed by observing the other.

beats.text: Two screens show related events. Looking at one screen lets you predict something about the other, so their uncertainty clouds overlap.
How many bits about Y do we gain, on average, when X is revealed?
Start with H(Y), then subtract the uncertainty that remains, H(Y|X). Equivalently compare H(X)+H(Y) with the joint entropy H(X,Y).
I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X). It is symmetric despite the conditional expression, nonnegative, and zero when X and Y are independent.
Mutual information is the reusable currency of a communication link: it quantifies shared predictive content without requiring a linear relationship.
Mutual information measures shared bits, equals entropy removed by a clue, and can be written H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).

visuals.title: Shared bits
visuals.goal: Make mutual information the overlap between two uncertainty sets.

visuals.title: Information Venn
visuals.goal: Track H(Y), H(Y|X), and their difference.

lessons.objective: By the end you can explain KL divergence as the extra average bits paid when coding P-generated data with Q.

beats.text: A map uses the wrong scale: every route is still possible, but the traveler repeatedly takes detours because the model's weights are off.
Can the cost of a wrong probability model be isolated from the source's unavoidable entropy?
Compare the cross-entropy bill H(P,Q) with the ideal entropy H(P). Their difference is the average penalty for Q's mismatch.
Dₖₗ(P‖Q)=H(P,Q)-H(P)=Σp(x)log₂[p(x)/q(x)]. It is nonnegative, zero only when P and Q agree, and asymmetric.
KL divergence is not a geometric distance, but it is a precise model-improvement signal: lower divergence means fewer wasted bits under the real source.
Subtract ideal entropy from cross-entropy to get extra bits. Keep the order P‖Q: reality supplies the average, Q supplies the code.

visuals.title: The wrong-map detour
visuals.goal: Show KL as wasted coding effort due to a model mismatch.

visuals.title: P versus Q cost
visuals.goal: Decompose cross-entropy into entropy plus divergence.

lessons.objective: By the end you can explain why redundancy helps a receiver correct noise and why reliable communication has a capacity limit.

beats.text: A message crosses a shaking tube. A few beads land in the wrong places, but a patterned message gives the receiver clues about what was intended.
How can extra structure protect information, and why can no clever code make an arbitrarily noisy channel perfect?
Separate compression from error correction: first remove predictable redundancy, then add carefully chosen redundancy so valid codewords remain distinguishable after noise.
A channel has a capacity: below the mutual-information limit, sufficiently long codes can make error probability small; above it, reliable transmission is impossible.
Entropy sets how much a source needs to say, mutual information measures what the channel conveys, and coding matches the rate to the channel's safe region.
Redundancy buys recoverability, noise consumes capacity, and Shannon's insight is an achievable reliable rate rather than a guarantee for every finite code.
